extracted.intended_audience: federal agency rulewriters and regulatory policy staff (and the informed public interested in rulemaking)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting federal regulations to comply with the Plain Writing Act and OIRA guidance, emphasizing an upfront executive summary and clearer presentation of key provisions, costs, and benefits to improve public participation and reduce compliance costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain Writing Act requirement: write in plain English
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are required by the Plain Writing Act of 2010 to write their regulations in plain English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that regulations should avoid 'gibberish' and complex language that makes it hard for the public to understand rules, provide input during comment periods, or comply. Plain language reduces the cost and difficulty of compliance and fosters open government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive summary: put the bottom line up front
rubrics_metrics.description: When publishing complicated rules, agencies should include an easy-to-understand executive summary that states the 'bottom line' up front.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA guidance and Sunstein argue that long, complex rules (sometimes over 1,000 pages) should begin with a concise statement of what the rule does so readers are not forced to wade through details to figure out required actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive summary component: state the purpose of the regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive summary should include the purpose of the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly articulate why the regulation exists and what problem it addresses, so the public can quickly grasp the rationale behind the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive summary component: summarize each major provision
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive summary should provide a summary of each major provision of the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For complex rules with multiple provisions, give brief, plain-language descriptions of each major element so readers can understand obligations and changes without parsing regulatory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive summary component: summarize costs and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive summary should include a summary of the costs and benefits associated with the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concise plain-language accounting of expected costs and benefits to help stakeholders assess impacts quickly and meaningfully during the comment period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight top provisions: list and emphasize five or six key provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the five or six key provisions of a rule and list them upfront, using typographic emphasis (italicized or bolded) to call them out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunstein suggests asking agencies to name the five or six key provisions and put them at the front—italicized or bold—so the public doesn't get lost in lengthy details (example: avoid getting lost in a 1,700-page regulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrospective review: review significant existing regulations for streamlining or repeal
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA is reviewing 'significant regulations' already on the books to identify which can be streamlined or repealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The retrospective review process should be as open to the public as possible; the goal is to reduce unnecessary complexity and burdens from existing regulations by identifying candidates for simplification or removal.
